## Human wavelength encoding overview {#sec-human-wavelength-encoding-overview}
Vision scientists have learned a great deal about the first stages of vision. We have excellent measurements of how the eye's optics (the cornea and lens) transform light from the world into an image on the retina, and we know how the retina's photoreceptors encode that image into neural signals. This knowledge serves as a practical guide for designing any system that reproduces images for people.

Consider color. A camera designed for human viewing should capture the same portion of the electromagnetic spectrum that we see: visible light. Capturing less of the spectrum would lead to poor color reproduction. Capturing more—like infrared or ultraviolet—would be wasteful, consuming resources to record information we can't see anyway. Worse yet, if we add in these signals into a reproduction the appearance would fail to match what we see.  Our knowledge of human wavelength sensitivity sets a clear target for an image system designed for consumer photography.

Spatial resolution presents a different challenge. It would be a disappointment if a camera failed to capture details as fine as those the human eye can resolve. We expect our photos to be at least as sharp as what we see. However, unlike color, people are generally pleased if a camera captures a scene at a *finer* resolution than the eye encodes. We zoom in on the digital image to see details we might have missed. This extra information doesn't interfere with the viewing experience; it just requires more storage and processing power.

So, we have two different engineering constraints derived from human vision:

*   **Wavelength:** Human vision sets a *target range*. 
*   **Spatial Resolution:** Human vision sets a *minimum bar*. 

In this section, we will review the way our visual system encodes wavelength and spatially samples the image.  Understanding the human visual system properties is good guidance for what we *cannot* see. This is essential knowledge for designing image systems intended for consumer photography.

## Color matching background
Thomas Young, giving the Bakerian lectures at the Royal Society in 1802 [@young1802-bakerian-light], directly explained why we should think that the 3-dimensionality of color -which was widely used in industry- was a property of the eye. But in the following years serious scientists, such as Brewster and Helmholtz, still made significant errors.  Brewster argued that light was of reduced dimensionality [@brewsterIVNewAnalysis1834]. Helmholtz accepted that the idea that biology was essential, but a flawed experimental analysis made him think that there are five, not three, color receptors in the eye [@helmholtzLXXXITheoryCompound1852][^color-history].  

[^color-history]: John Mollon wrote an excellent chapter describing the history of color vision [@mollon2003-Origins-Color]. There is much to be learned from his historical account. I draw the reader's attention to how much was known implicitly by commercial firms prior to Maxwell's scientific analysis. The exchange between commerce and science is present throughout the field of image systems and far beyond. As Lawrence J. Henderson is said to have put it, "Science owes more to the steam engine than the steam engine owes to science" [@gillispie1960-edge-objectivity, p. 357].


::: {.callout-note title="The trials and redemption of Thomas Young" collapse="true"}
When Thomas Young delivered his landmark Bakerian Lectures to the Royal Society between 1801 and 1803 [@young1802-bakerian-light; @young1804-bakerian-optics], he boldly introduced two ideas that fundamentally challenged orthodoxy: first, that light travels as an undulatory wave governed by the principle of interference; and second, that the presence of a continuous spectrum of waves means human color vision must be trichromatic because the retina possesses three distinct sensor mechanisms, not because the physical signal itself is trichromatic.

At the time, the British scientific establishment was fiercely devoted to Sir Isaac Newton’s corpuscular (particle) theory of light and opposed the wave theory. To question Newton was seen not merely as a scientific disagreement, but as an act of national and intellectual heresy. 

Enter Henry Brougham, a dogmatic disciple of Newton's corpuscular framework and co-founder of the influential *Edinburgh Review*, who launched a broadside against Young in its pages with a series of caustic, personal attacks:

> ...this paper contains nothing which deserves the name, either of experiment or of discovery, and as it is, in fact, destitute of every species of merit. We now dismiss, for the present, the feeble lucubrations[^lucubrations] of this author, in which we have searched without success for some traces of learning, acuteness, and ingenuity, that might compensate his evident deficiency in the powers of solid thinking, calm and patient investigation … 

[^lucubrations]: In 18th- and 19th-century English, a *lucubration* meant pedantic, late-night candlelit scribbling. Brougham was accusing Young of armchair speculation—fanciful daydreaming by candlelight rather than the rigorous, empirical work of a true natural philosopher.

Brougham treated Young's undulatory hypothesis—which revived ideas first championed by Christiaan Huygens—as a betrayal of Newton’s legacy. An amateur scientist, he spent substantial effort attempting to force diffraction into a corpuscular model of particles deflecting around obstacles. Being in an intellectual cult is something we should all try to avoid.

Young was a gentleman scholar and a practicing London physician. In 1804, he published a dignified pamphlet in his own defense—*A Reply to the Animadversions of the Edinburgh Reviewers* [@young1804-reply]:

> A MAN who has a proper regard for the dignity of his own character, although his sensibility may sometimes be awakened by the unjust attacks of interested malevolence, will esteem it in general more advisable to bear, in silence, the temporary effects of a short-lived injury, than to suffer his own pursuits to be interrupted, in making an effort to repel the invective, and to punish the aggressor.

Young printed 1,000 copies of his defense at his own expense. Reportedly, **only a single copy was sold**. 
Meanwhile, the *Edinburgh Review* was circulating to thousands of Britain's educated elite. 

In Regency London, a physician accused in print of flighty, ungrounded speculation faced professional ruin; patients would not trust their health to an "unstable" theorist. Young’s authority was badly shaken, and he resigned his professorship of Natural Philosophy at the Royal Institution. Deeply bruised and isolated, Young largely withdrew from public optical debate for more than a decade. He turned his extraordinary polymathic intellect elsewhere: deciphering Egyptian hieroglyphs on the Rosetta Stone, writing medical treatises, and developing insurance mathematics. 

More than 200 years later, this still pisses me off.

History was not finished with Thomas Young. In the twilight of the Napoleonic Wars (around 1814–1815), a young French civil engineer named Augustin-Jean Fresnel began experimenting on diffraction in Normandy. Cut off from British journals by war, and with Young's papers buried by Brougham's derision, Fresnel independently rediscovered the wave nature and interference of light.

When François Arago reviewed Fresnel’s findings at the Académie des Sciences in Paris, he realized that an English physician had anticipated many of these principles more than a decade earlier. Rather than sparking nationalistic rivalry, Arago and Fresnel reached out to Young. Fresnel openly credited Young with discovering the principle of interference, initiating a warm and generous correspondence.

The exchange bore extraordinary fruit. When Arago and Fresnel discovered that light beams polarized at right angles do not interfere—a puzzle impossible to explain if light waves were longitudinal, like sound—Young had another crucial leap of intuition in 1817: he suggested that light waves might be *transverse*, oscillating perpendicular to the direction of propagation, like the ripples on a plucked string (I discuss the physics of transverse waves and polarization in @sec-optics-polarization). 

Fresnel embraced Young's insight and built the rigorous mathematical mechanics of transverse waves. His equations beautifully accounted for polarization, double refraction, and diffraction. When the staunch Newtonian judge Siméon Denis Poisson argued that Fresnel's equations led to the "absurd" consequence that a bright spot must appear in the very center of a circular shadow, Arago promptly conducted the experiment and observed the bright spot (the famous Poisson/Arago spot recounted in @sec-evidence-wave-theory), handing wave theory a decisive victory over corpuscles.

Young’s vindication was complete. His detractors were silenced, not by polemics, but by the mathematical and experimental triumph of the theory he had pioneered. The mutual respect between Young and Fresnel became one of the most generous partnerships in the history of science. Young wrote of Fresnel:

> Fresnel earned his success by his labor; he took the theory up where I left it, and carried it on to a degree of perfection to which I could never have brought it.[^young-fresnel]

In 1827, the Royal Society awarded Fresnel its highest honor, the Rumford Medal. As Foreign Secretary of the Royal Society, Young had the bittersweet privilege of writing to inform Fresnel of the prize. Fresnel, dying of tuberculosis at thirty-nine, received the medal just days before his death. He wrote back that receiving the esteem of Young and his peers was far dearer to him than any fleeting fame.

[^young-fresnel]: Thomas Young’s letter to François Arago, January 12, 1817 (quoted in Arago’s *Éloge historique du Dr. Thomas Young* and collected in George Peacock’s 1855 *Life of Thomas Young*).

[More on this historical episode can be found in Nahum's analysis](https://www.qeios.com/read/LJ7AGZ).
:::

My enthusiasm for Maxwell is based on the fact that he settled, once and for all, the question of the biological basis of trichromacy. Moreover, he did so in a way that established a clear conceptual structure that we still use today[@maxwell1857-XVIIIExperimentsColourPerceived; @maxwell1860-IVTheoryCompound]. Beyond theory, he collaborated with Thomas Sutton to produce the first color photographs [@fig-maxwell-sutton], demonstrating that his understanding was true and useful [@Sutton1861-color; @maxwell1861-three-primary][^feynman-maxwell]. 

[^feynman-maxwell]: I think of Feynman's comment, "What I cannot create, I do not understand". Maxwell created.

Maxwell did the color work just prior to taking on the challenges of unifying the equations for electicity and magnetism and discovering that light is also electromagnetic radiation. I am so pleased that color science can call Maxwell one of our own.

Mollon’s reading of Palmer’s 1777 tract (Theory of Colours and Vision) and his subsequent 1781/1786 writings reveals a mix of prescient biological intuition and physical error:

What Palmer actually asserted: Palmer proposed that the retina possesses three distinct types of particles, fibres, or membranes (corresponding to red, yellow, and blue), and that equal stimulation of all three gives rise to the perception of white. In 1781 (writing under the pseudonym Giros von Gentilly), he extended this to argue that color blindness occurs when one or two of these three molecular classes are missing or inactive—which Mollon notes as arguably the earliest proposal of an inherited receptor-level defect.

The caveat: Palmer did not deduce trichromacy from quantitative color matching, nor did he realize that physical light is a continuous distribution of wavelengths. You are entirely correct to point that out. The mistake in the earlier account mischaracterized both the yellow match (which works additively) and the actual logic Helmholtz employed in his 1852 paper.

Here is a revised, accurate historical review centering on how color matching developed, the specific conceptual mistake Helmholtz made, and how Maxwell resolved it.

---

### 1. Color Matching Before Maxwell: Empirical Craft vs. Additive Tests

Before Maxwell’s quantitative colorimetry in the 1850s, the notion of three-dimensionality existed primarily as an industrial rule of thumb, along with a handful of qualitative optical experiments:

* **The Practical / Subtractive Tradition:** Early printers and painters knew empirically that a small palette of pigments could span the gamut of hues. Jacob Christoph Le Blon (1710s–1720s) commercialized three-color mezzotint printing using red, yellow, and blue inks. Tobias Mayer (1758) and Johann Heinrich Lambert (1772) later formalized pigment mixtures into triangular color solids. However, these subtractive mixtures conflated pigment physics with light mixture, entrenching the mistaken belief that green light was physically composed of yellow and blue light.
* **Christian Ernst Wünsch (1792):** As John Mollon has documented, Wünsch conducted the first decisive additive mixture experiments using prisms to isolate and superimpose spectral bands. He proved that spectral red and spectral green additively produce yellow, and identified red, green, and violet as the true fundamental lights.
* **Thomas Young (1801–1802):** Young took the critical step of shifting trichromacy from an assumed property of light to a property of human physiology. Because light spans an infinite physical spectrum, the eye cannot possess infinite resonators; Young asserted that the retina contains three types of sensitive nerve fibers (red, green, violet). Young’s hypothesis, however, remained an untested physical-physiological conjecture; he performed no systematic color-matching experiments to prove that all colors could be represented in a 3D linear space.

Remember that Brewster still thought color was a physical property.  Maxwell did some simple, decisive experiments by interposing a filter on metamers to show that they transmitted differently and thus the lights were not the same.  They only appeared to be the same and thus the color matches were biological, not physical.

---

### 2. Helmholtz’s 1852 Logic: Segmenting the Spectrum

When Hermann von Helmholtz took up the problem in his 1852 paper (*Über die Theorie der zusammengesetzten Farben*), he set out to test Newton’s color circle and Young’s hypothesis using a V-shaped slit and prism apparatus to superimpose pairs of narrow spectral bands:

* **The Stepping Procedure:** Rather than attempting three-variable color matching, Helmholtz fixed one spectral wavelength and gradually moved a second wavelength further away along the spectrum, mixing them to see whether intermediate spectral hues could be reproduced.
* **The Failure of Two-Wavelength Segments:** As soon as the two wavelengths were separated by more than a certain interval, their mixture could no longer match the appearance of the wavelengths between them. By continuing this "stepping" across the visible range, Helmholtz partitioned the spectrum into **five distinct segments**: red, yellow, green, blue, and violet.
* **The Flawed Premise:** Underlying Helmholtz’s reasoning was the assumption that each primary sensation operated essentially in isolation—that a pure, monochromatic wavelength was detected by one primary element at a time. If mixing the end-points of a segment failed to capture the sensations inside the next, he concluded that Young’s three-receptor scheme was insufficient and that the eye must require **at least five primary sensations** (or a continuum of them).

---

### 3. Grassmann’s Mathematics and Maxwell’s Resolution

The breakthrough came from abandoning Helmholtz's assumption of independent, segmented primary channels:

* **Hermann Grassmann (1853):** Grassmann recognized that Helmholtz’s experimental logic violated basic linear geometry. Grassmann showed theoretically that if color matching obeyed three basic rules (superposition, homogeneity, and transitivity), any human color sensation could be represented as an element in a **three-dimensional vector space**. Grassmann argued that Helmholtz’s failure to reproduce spectral colors with two-primary steps did not disprove trichromacy; rather, it arose from treating color mixture as piecewise combinations rather than simultaneous vector mixtures of three primaries.

* **Maxwell’s Coterminal Curves (1855–1860):** Maxwell grasped what Helmholtz had missed: **the eye’s sensitive elements must have broad, overlapping spectral sensitivities**. Under this framework, light at any single wavelength (such as 580 nm) simultaneously stimulates multiple receptor classes in a fixed ratio. Mixing a spectral red and a spectral green stimulates those same classes in that exact same ratio, producing a complete perceptual match to 580 nm.

* **Maxwell's Quantitative Metric:** Using spinning tops and his calibrated color box, Maxwell carried out the world's first true quantitative color-matching experiments, determining the linear color-matching functions and proving that human color vision is strictly three-dimensional.

* **Helmholtz’s Conversion:** Convinced by Grassmann’s linear formulation and Maxwell’s empirical measurements, Helmholtz retracted his five-primary interpretation. In his *Handbuch der physiologischen Optik* (1860), he embraced Young’s three-receptor framework combined with Maxwell’s overlapping broadband sensitivities, synthesizing it with Johannes Müller's law of specific nerve energies into the modern Young–Helmholtz theory.
